opus-5.5.text:
I think about it less as a balance and more as a sequencing problem. People often frame it as a tug-of-war: every hour on research is an hour not spent on revenue, and vice versa. In our case, the scientific ambition is the commercial thesis. We're betting that if you can build AI systems that genuinely reason mathematically, and can prove their outputs are correct rather than just sounding plausible, that capability becomes extremely valuable. It matters to mathematicians, and also anywhere correctness matters: software verification, chip design, finance, any domain where a subtle error is very costly.

So the question I ask isn't "science or business?" It's "which scientific milestones unlock which commercial doors, and in what order?" Some problems are beautiful but don't compound into anything. Others are a bit less glamorous, like building better infrastructure for formal languages, data pipelines, or tooling for verification. They aren't headline results, but every later capability gets built on top of them. We try to prioritize work that is both scientifically meaningful and load-bearing for the product.

That said, I'd be lying if I said there's no tension. As a founder you feel it every day. There's always a temptation to chase a near-term customer request that pulls you sideways. There's also the opposite temptation, especially for people like me from a math background: to disappear into a hard problem for a year because it's intellectually irresistible. I try to guard against both.

A few things help. First, we're very explicit internally about our long-term north star, so when an opportunity comes up we can ask whether it moves us toward that or is a detour. Second, we hire people who care about both. Researchers who enjoy seeing their work used in the real world, and engineers who appreciate why rigor matters. That cultural overlap does a lot of the balancing for you. Third, I think it's important to be honest with investors and the team about timelines. Deep technical work takes time, and pretending otherwise creates bad incentives.

And honestly, there's a deeper reason I care about this. Mathematics has always been one of humanity's purest pursuits. If we can build tools that help mathematicians go further, and those same tools make the software and systems we rely on more trustworthy, that's a rare case where doing good science and building a good business point in the same direction. My job is to keep them pointed that way.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think of them as being in tension, honestly, at least not at the stage we're at. The whole premise of Axiom is that the scientific problem is the commercial problem. If we can build a system that actually reasons mathematically, that can formalize a conjecture, search for a proof, verify it rigorously, and do that at a level that matters to working mathematicians, then the applications follow from that. Verified software, cryptography, financial modeling, anything where correctness is non-negotiable. You can't fake your way to those markets with a model that's merely plausible. So the science is the moat.

Where I do feel the tension is in time horizons and in what you choose to measure. It's very tempting in this field to optimize for a benchmark number or a demo that looks impressive, because that's what raises money and that's what gets attention. And some of that is necessary. But a lot of the deepest progress in mathematics doesn't show up on a leaderboard for a long time. Formalizing something in Lean, building the infrastructure so a model can check its own work, that's slow and unglamorous and it doesn't produce a headline. I spend a lot of my energy protecting that kind of work from being crowded out.

The way I try to balance it practically is to be very honest internally about which bets are which. Some things we do because they'll produce value in six months, and we say so. Some things we do because we believe they're true about how mathematical intelligence has to work, and we'd do them even if nobody paid us for a while. As long as the team knows which is which, and the people funding us know which is which, you avoid the worst failure mode, which is pretending a long-term scientific bet is a short-term product and then being disappointed by both.

And I'd add one more thing. I came out of pure mathematics, and mathematicians are trained to be suspicious of anything that's useful too quickly. I've had to unlearn some of that. Commercial pressure, when it's the right kind, actually sharpens the science. It forces you to ask whether the problem you're solving is real, whether anyone would notice if you solved it. That's a good question for a mathematician to ask too.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is finding a commercial problem where solving it actually requires meaningful scientific progress. Then the two ambitions can reinforce each other: the science gives you a way to build something valuable, and the commercial work gives you feedback about whether it’s useful.

But they don’t always move on the same timeline. You need room for research whose payoff is uncertain, while also being clear about what you can deliver to a customer today. I’d want us to be ambitious about the long-term direction and disciplined about the promises we make along the way.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make scientific ambition and commercial priorities inform each other. You need a long-term view of what could become possible, but you also need a clear sense of whose problem you’re solving and why they would pay for it.

In practice, I’d distinguish between work that needs room for uncertainty and work that needs to deliver reliably. Research shouldn’t have to justify itself through immediate revenue every week. But it should have milestones that help us learn whether an approach is promising. And on the commercial side, customer feedback can reveal scientific problems we might otherwise overlook.

The balance isn’t fixed. Sometimes you need to push further on the science; sometimes you need to focus and turn what already works into something useful. The important thing is being honest about which stage you’re in.
